code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: payments
  name: pod-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
caption: apiGroups + resources + verbs is the whole grammar of an RBAC rule.

steps.label: Role / ClusterRole
steps.sub: define WHAT is allowed — namespaced vs. cluster-scoped or reusable

steps.label: RoleBinding
steps.sub: grants a Role, or a ClusterRole scoped down, inside one namespace

steps.label: ClusterRoleBinding
steps.sub: grants a ClusterRole across the entire cluster — handle with care

eyebrow: A dedicated ServiceAccount for a workload
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: billing-reader
  namespace: payments
---
kind: RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: payments
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: billing-reader
    namespace: payments
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
caption: Give every workload its own identity instead of sharing the namespace's default ServiceAccount.

eyebrow: Checking before you find out the hard way
code:
kubectl auth can-i delete pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:billing-reader -n payments
no

kubectl auth can-i --list \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:billing-reader -n payments
caption: kubectl auth can-i asks the real authorizer — no guessing about what a binding actually grants.

subtitle: Who a Pod can call is only half of workload security — what it's allowed to do once it's running is the other half.
